exp.1:12:
This verse says that you were once far away from God, but now, because you are united with Christ Jesus, God has brought you near. He did this by the blood of Christ, that is, by his death on the cross. The word "you" here means all of you as a group, and being "made nigh" means that you now have access to God.

Paul is writing to believers who were not Jews (Gentiles). He reminds them that they were once outside the promises made to Israel, without hope and without knowing God. He then explains that Christ broke down the wall that separated Jews and Gentiles, to form one people living in peace.

For today: if God has brought you near through Christ, you do not need to earn his affection or feel distant from him. Pray with confidence. And just as Christ broke down walls, seek to draw close to people who are different from you, without contempt or division.
exp.1:14:
This verse says that Jesus, through his own body on the cross, ended the hostility between two groups. The word "abolished" means to bring to an end or put a stop to. "The law of commandments contained in ordinances" refers to the rules and ceremonies of the law of Moses that kept Jews and non-Jews apart. Christ made the two into one new people, a new community, and so brought peace.

Paul writes to Christians of non-Jewish background in Ephesus. He wants them to understand that they are no longer strangers, but part of the same people of God together with the believers who were Jewish.

Commentators explain in different ways how the law is "abolished" here, but they all agree that Christ removed the barrier that divided.

For today: if Christ made one people, we must not build walls based on origin, culture or customs. This week, approach a brother or sister in the faith who is very different from you with respect and friendship.
exp.4:17:
This verse tells us not to get drunk with wine, because that leads to a life that is wild, out of control, and going to ruin. Instead, Paul invites us to be filled with the Spirit, that is, to let the Holy Spirit guide and govern our lives.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Ephesus. Earlier he asked them to make good use of their time and not to be foolish, but to understand what the Lord wants. Then he shows what that fullness looks like: singing, praising, and giving thanks to God together.

For today: instead of looking for relief or joy in things that control us, such as alcohol or other excesses, we can ask each day for the Spirit to guide us. This shows in gratitude, in praise, and in how we treat others.
exp.4:13:
This verse is an urgent invitation: wake up from spiritual sleep, rise from the dead, and receive the light of Christ. The word "exposed" means reproved or brought into the open. The word "shines" means gives light or illuminates.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus. He has just spoken to them about leaving the works of darkness and living as children of light. He introduces a quotation with the words "for this reason it says," so he is citing something, but it is not known with certainty where it comes from. Some think it is an early Christian hymn or song, and others think it summarizes passages from Isaiah. There is no certain agreement. What is clear is that it calls people to come out of a life without God.

Today, if you notice that you have grown used to something that pulls you away from God, do not hide it. Bring it into the light in prayer, confess it, and take one concrete step today to change. Christ promises to shine on you.
exp.4:12:
It says that when wrong deeds are "reproved" (that is, rebuked or brought out into the open), the light lets them be seen as they really are. The reason is simple: light has the property of making visible everything it touches.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus. He asks them not to take part in the dark deeds of those who live without God, but to expose them, not with pride, but by living in a different way. Then he quotes some words (their exact origin is debated) that invite people to wake up and receive the light of Christ.

Today we can live with sincerity and kindness, without hiding anything. If something hidden weighs on us, let us bring it to Christ and to someone we trust. Our honest life can be a gentle light that helps others see.
exp.0:22:
It says the church is the body of Christ, and that she is the "fulness" of him who "filleth" (that is, fills) all things in all. Christ is the head, and the church is his body. Scholars understand "fulness" in several ways: the church is where Christ is made present and shown, or it is what Christ fills with his life. The exact sense is debated.

Paul writes this letter, probably from prison, to believers who knew little of their place in God's plan. He has just spoken of the power by which God raised Christ and set him over all power and every name. Now he wants them to see that this exalted Christ is united to his church.

For today: do not see your faith as something only private. You are part of a body that Christ fills. Seek out a community of believers, serve in it with what you have, and value the other members.
exp.5:14:
It says that the believer should have their feet well shod with the readiness of the gospel of peace. "Readiness" means preparation, being prepared, or firmness for action. It is like putting on good footwear before setting out on a difficult road. The gospel of peace is the message that God reconciles us to Himself through Jesus.

Paul writes this letter, probably from prison, to the Christians in Ephesus. He uses the image of a Roman soldier to teach them to stand firm against evil. Scholars explain this footwear in different ways: as stability for standing firm, or as readiness to carry the good news. Both ideas fit.

For today: before beginning the day, ask God to establish you in his peace. That way you can remain calm in difficulties and be ready to share a word of hope with someone who needs it.
exp.2:18:
It says we can come to know the love of Christ, although that love is so great that no mind can fully grasp it. The word "exceeds" means that it surpasses or is greater. Your reader's verse uses "passeth knowledge" for this idea. The purpose of this knowing is that we may be filled with all the fulness of God, that is, that God fills our lives with what He is.

The speaker is the apostle Paul, who is writing to the believers in Ephesus. This is part of a prayer of his for them. He asks that Christ may dwell in their hearts and that they may be rooted deeply in love. This prayer ends with praise to God.

For today: knowing facts about Jesus is not enough. Set aside a few minutes each day to meditate on his love, for example by reading a passage from the Gospels, and thank him for something specific.
exp.2:0:
Paul calls himself "the prisoner of Jesus Christ" and says he is one "for you Gentiles," that is, for you who are not Jews. "For this cause" points back to what he has just explained in chapter 2. The words here are plain: "you" refers to the readers, and "Gentiles" are the non-Jewish nations.

Paul writes from prison, probably in Rome, though some think it was another place. He says his imprisonment belongs to Christ, not only to the authorities, because he is there for preaching that the Gentiles are also part of God's people. The sentence is left unfinished, and he picks up the thought again later, in verse 14.

For today: when we serve God and it costs us something, we can see it as part of our calling and not as a loss. God can use our difficulties to bless others.
exp.4:27:
It says that husbands should love their wives with the same care with which they look after their own bodies. The word "so" points back to what came before: Christ's love for the church. The older forms "á" and "a" are the same word, so no difference is intended. And "he that loveth his wife loveth himself" means that in marriage the two are so united that the good of one is the good of the other.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just described how Christ gave himself for the church to cleanse her and present her holy. Now he uses that example to teach husbands to love with self-giving and not with domination. The verses that follow explain it: no one hates his own body, but feeds and cares for it, as Christ does with his church.

Today, a husband might ask himself, "How do I look after my own health and needs?" He can then give that same effort to listening to, serving, and protecting his wife, with concrete actions every day.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that sexual immorality, all impurity, and greed should not even be mentioned among believers, because they do not belong with those who belong to God. "Sexual immorality" is any sexual sin outside God's design; "impurity" is every kind of uncleanness; "greed" is the desire to have more at any cost. The word "saints" refers to those whom God has set apart for himself, that is, believers.

The apostle Paul is writing to the church in Ephesus. He has just asked them to imitate God and to live in love, as Christ gave himself up for them. Now he shows them the opposite of love: using others or things for one's own desires. He then warns that whoever lives this way has no inheritance in the kingdom.

Today we can examine what we see, say, and desire. If something feeds selfishness or impurity, let us ask God for help to change it and to practice gratitude.
exp.2:5:
What it says: Paul explains the "mystery": the non-Jews (Gentiles) are now fellow heirs with Israel, members of the same body, and sharers in God's promise. Being "fellow heirs" means they receive the same inheritance; being part of "the same body" means they belong to the same body; being "partakers" means they share together in what is promised. All of this is in Christ, through the gospel.

Context: Paul writes while imprisoned for preaching to the Gentiles, to a church made up of both Jews and non-Jews. He wants them to understand that this plan, not made known with such clarity before, has now been revealed to the apostles and prophets. He presents himself as a servant of that grace.

For today: In Christ no one is a second-class Christian. Today you can welcome every person in your church with joy, regardless of their background, culture or past, because God received them just as he received you.
exp.4:19:
This verse invites us to give thanks to God at all times and for all things. We do this by addressing God as Father, and in the name of Jesus Christ. "Always for all things" means on every occasion and in every circumstance.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus. Earlier he spoke about being filled with the Spirit rather than with wine. That Spirit-filled life shows itself in singing, in praise, and in thankfulness. He then adds that we should submit to one another, so gratitude also shapes how we treat people. Some scholars debate whether "all things" includes the pain itself or only what God does in the midst of it.

Today you can begin or end your day by naming three specific things you are thankful to God for. Do this even on difficult days, trusting that the Father cares for you through Christ.
exp.2:17:
Paul asks that believers may be able to grasp fully, together with all the other Christians, "the breadth, and length, and depth, and height." The verse does not say what these measures refer to, but the text that follows suggests it is the love of Christ. Here "length" is the same as the word "long" in ordinary speech, and "comprehend" means to understand something thoroughly.

Paul writes this letter to the Ephesians and is praying for them. He asks that the Spirit strengthen them inwardly, that Christ may dwell in their hearts through faith, and that they be rooted and grounded in love. Interpreters explain the four measures in various ways, but nearly all of them see them as a way of expressing how immense the love of Christ is.

Today, let us not try to grow in faith alone. We understand the love of Christ better within the community of believers. Seek out other Christians to pray with, read the Bible with, and share what God is teaching you.
exp.0:17:
Paul asks that God would "enlighten" the eyes of the heart, that is, that he would give light to the mind and to the inner life of believers. In this way they will be able to understand three things: the hope to which God has called them (the word "calling" here means the summons or invitation), the riches of the glory of God's inheritance, and what it means for the saints, the people of God, to be part of that inheritance. The "saints" are the believers set apart for God.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus, probably from prison. He tells them that he prays for them with thankfulness. He does not ask them for more information, but that God would give them spiritual understanding so that they may know him better. Some scholars wonder whether "his inheritance" refers to what God gives to the saints or to what God receives in them; the text allows both readings.

For today: pray asking God to help you understand his love and his hope, not only to know facts about him. That hope can sustain you in difficult days.
exp.4:18:
It says that Christians should encourage one another with psalms (songs taken from the Bible), hymns (songs of praise to God), and spiritual songs (songs inspired by the Spirit). Speaking to one another means encouraging one another. And the phrase in your hearts indicates that the singing should come from within, with sincerity, and not only from the lips.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Ephesus. Earlier he told them not to be drunk with wine, but to be filled with the Spirit. This Spirit-filled life shows itself in singing, in thankfulness, and in humility toward one another. Scholars debate whether each of the song terms points to a different kind of song, or whether they are used in a broad sense.

For today: sing or listen to music that carries the truth of God, and use it to encourage your family or your church, with a grateful heart.
exp.3:21:
This verse says that believers must leave behind their former way of living. The "old self" is the person we were before we knew Christ, with damaged habits and customs. "Corrupt" means spoiled or ruined by sin, and the "deceitful desires" are the misleading longings that lead people down the wrong path. The old form of the word "to" is written differently in older texts, but in the verse you read it is simply "to."

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians of Ephesus, many of whom came from a pagan background. He reminds them that what they learned from Christ does not go together with the life they lived before. That is why the change is not optional: it is part of following Jesus. The verses that follow explain that it is not only a matter of giving something up, but also of receiving a new life.

For today: think about one habit or thought that pulls you away from God, such as lying, constant complaining, or anger. Ask God for help to let it go, and replace it with something good, such as telling the truth or giving thanks.
exp.4:32:
This verse sums up what Paul taught before. Each husband should love his wife as he loves himself, that is, care for her and seek her good. And the wife should reverence her husband, or in other words, respect and honor him.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just spoken about marriage and compared it to the union of Christ and the church. With this verse he closes that teaching and directs it to each person individually.

For today: think of one concrete way to love or respect your spouse this week, such as listening carefully or thanking them for their efforts. If you are not married, you can apply the same spirit of love and respect in your close relationships.
exp.0:18:
Here Paul says that God's power toward those who believe is immensely great, so great that it surpasses every measure. The word "exceeding" means that it goes beyond everything known. He uses several words for power together (power, working, strength, might) to stress that this force is real and active, not merely an idea.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus, probably from prison. He tells them that he prays for God to open the eyes of their heart so that they understand their hope and their inheritance. Then he explains that this same power raised Christ from the dead, as the following verse says.

For today: when you feel weak or without a way out, remember that the power that raised Jesus acts on behalf of those who believe. Pray asking God to help you trust in that strength, and take a step of obedience today even if you feel small.
exp.3:17:
This verse says that people who live far from God have their minds darkened, that is, filled with darkness, like someone who cannot see the way clearly. They are separated from the life that comes from God. Paul points to two causes: ignorance (not knowing or wanting to understand the truth of God) and a hardened heart (a closed, stubborn heart that no longer responds).

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus, most of whom were not Jewish by origin. He asks them not to live as the Gentiles did, who followed empty thinking. He wants the church to grow united in love, like a body, and so he reminds them that they have learned Christ in a different way.

For today: when you notice that your heart is becoming hard or indifferent, draw near to God with humility. Read his Word and ask him to open your understanding and soften your heart.
exp.0:12:
The Ephesians, like the first Jewish believers, heard the true message, the gospel that brings salvation, and placed their hope in Christ. When they believed, God marked them with the Holy Spirit, whom he had promised. Here "trusted" means to put your confidence in someone, and "sealed" speaks of a mark of belonging and security.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus, most of whom were not Jewish. In the verses before, he speaks of "we," the first ones to hope in Christ, and now he says "you," including the Gentiles. He wants them to see that they too fully belong to God. The next verse calls the Spirit a guarantee, that is, an advance pledge of the inheritance to come.

For today: if you have believed in Christ, your security does not rest on your feelings or your performance, but on the fact that God himself has set his seal on you. Today you can live with peace and gratitude, trusting in his promise.
exp.2:16:
Paul says that Christ may dwell in the hearts of believers through faith. The word "dwell" means to settle in and make one's home there, as in one's own house, not merely to visit. "Rooted" speaks of roots that hold up a tree, and "grounded" of foundations that hold up a building. Love is the soil and the base of the Christian life.

Paul writes this letter, probably from prison. Here he prays for the believers, asking that God strengthen them through his Spirit in their inner being. He wants them, rooted and grounded in love, to be able to grasp better how great the love of Christ is. This prayer continues in the verses that follow.

For today: trust in Christ as someone who lives with you, not far from you. When you feel insecure or tired, remember that your roots are in his love. Set aside a moment each day to pray and thank him for being present in your life.
exp.0:1:
Paul greets his readers by wishing that "grace" and "peace" reach them. "Grace" is the undeserved favor of God, and "peace" is the calm and well-being that come from being right with Him. According to the verse, these two things come from God the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ.

Paul writes this letter as an apostle, that is, one sent by Christ, to the believers at Ephesus. This greeting was his usual way of beginning his letters. Some scholars think the letter may have circulated among other churches as well, because some ancient manuscripts do not include the words "at Ephesus." After the greeting, Paul begins to praise God for His blessings.

Today we can begin the day by remembering that grace and peace are not earned: they are received from God. Before we worry about what we have to do, we can ask Him to give us both.
exp.4:4:
It says that those who live in sexual immorality, impurity, or greed have no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God. A "whoremonger" is someone who practices sexual immorality; an "unclean person" is the impure one; a "covetous man" is the greedy one. Paul says the covetous man is an "idolater," because he puts money or what he desires in the place of God. "Inheritance" means having a share in the kingdom.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus. Earlier he asked that such things not even be named among them, as is fitting for holy people. He warns them that no one should deceive them with empty words. Interpreters debate how this fits with grace: some see a warning to those who call themselves believers yet remain in this way of life; others see a description of those who have never been transformed.

Today: examine what desire rules your heart. Ask God for help to leave whatever dominates you and to live with gratitude.
exp.5:12:
Paul tells the believers to put on the whole armor that God gives. To "withstand" means not giving way or backing down in the face of attack. "The evil day" is a time of testing or heavy pressure. "Having done all" can be understood as having done everything that is needed, or as having overcome everything; scholars interpret it in both ways. The goal is to remain standing.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Ephesus, probably while he is in prison. He reminds them that the deeper struggle is not against people, but against spiritual forces of evil. That is why their own strength is not enough: they need what God provides, such as truth, righteousness, peace, and faith, which are mentioned right after this.

For today: when difficult days come, do not wait until the crisis arrives. Right now, every day, seek God in prayer and in his Word, and stay rooted in the truth. In this way you will be prepared to keep standing firm.
exp.0:13:
The Holy Spirit is described as the earnest of our inheritance. An earnest is a first installment, a down payment that guarantees the rest will arrive. "Redemption of the purchased possession" refers to the final deliverance of the people God has bought for himself. All of this happens "unto the praise of his glory": in the end, God receives the honor.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus, in a letter that praises God for the spiritual blessings in Christ. He reminds them that, when they believed the gospel, they were marked with the Spirit, like a seal of belonging. Then he goes on to give thanks for their faith and their love.

For today: when you doubt your future with God, remember that his Spirit in you is a guarantee, not a mere hope. Rest in that certainty and live thankfully, seeking that your life honors God.
exp.5:2:
It says the promise of honoring parents is that a person will prosper and have a long life on the earth. "That it may" shows the result or purpose of that honor. "That it may be well with thee" means that life is good and prosperous, and "long life" refers to living many years.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Ephesus. Here he quotes the fifth commandment of the law of Moses (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16) and applies it to Christian children. It is part of his teaching about family life. Scholars understand the promise as a general principle of wisdom, not as an absolute guarantee for every person.

For today: honor your parents with respect, gratitude, and attention, even as an adult. It can be a phone call, a visit, or listening to their advice with humility. If the relationship is difficult, honoring them can begin with prayer and dignified treatment, without accepting mistreatment.
exp.2:12:
Paul asks the Ephesians not to lose heart or grow discouraged because of the sufferings he is going through. He explains that his sufferings are "your glory," meaning something that brings honor to them.

Paul writes from prison, held for preaching that non-Jews are also part of God's plan. His sufferings come from serving them. For this reason he reminds them that, in Christ, they have security and confident access to God. After this encouragement, Paul begins to pray for them.

For today: when you see someone suffering for serving God and others, do not lose heart or think that everything was in vain. God can use faithful suffering to bless many. Pray for those who serve with sacrifice, and trust that Christ sustains your faith.
exp.0:14:
Therefore the apostle Paul says that, because of everything he has just explained about the blessings God gives to believers, he has heard something good about them: that they have faith in the Lord Jesus and love all the saints. Here "saints" means the believers, the people of God, and "heard" means that news about them reached him.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus. After speaking of how God sealed them with the Holy Spirit, he now moves on to give thanks and to pray for them. Some scholars think the letter circulated among several churches, and that is why it sounds so general. His joy comes from seeing that faith and love go together.

For today: a true faith in Jesus shows itself in love toward other believers. Today you can give thanks to God for someone in your church and show that love with a message, a visit, or a concrete help.
exp.4:16:
It tells us not to live without thinking, like someone who acts without reflection, but to seek to understand what the will of the Lord is. "Unwise" here means foolish or careless. "Understanding" means grasping clearly with good judgment.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus. Earlier he asked them to walk carefully, as wise people, making good use of the time, because the days are evil. Then he contrasts a life without control, such as drunkenness, with a life filled with the Spirit, which is expressed in praise and fellowship. Understanding the will of God, then, is part of living wisely.

For today: before deciding something important, take a moment to pray and seek God's guidance in his Word. Ask yourself whether that decision honors him, and ask for counsel from mature believers.
exp.3:25:
This verse says that we can feel anger, but we must not let it lead us to do wrong. "Be angry" means "be angry," and "sin not" means "do not sin." And "let not the sun go down upon your wrath" means that we should not hold on to anger until the day is over, but should deal with it soon.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus. After speaking about the new self, he gives examples of how to live differently: put away lying, speak the truth, and care for unity, because we are members of one another. Then he warns that anger handled badly can give the devil an opening. Some think the phrase about the sun is a practical expression, not an exact time.

Today, if something has upset you, speak calmly, forgive, or seek reconciliation before you go to sleep, so that bitterness does not grow in your heart.
exp.1:20:
He says that Jesus Christ is the main cornerstone of God's building. The word for "fitly framed together" means joined together and well fitted, like stones that fit snugly with one another. That building is not finished; it keeps on growing. Its goal is to become a holy temple, meaning a place set apart for God, and all of this happens in the Lord, because we are united with Christ.

Paul writes this letter to believers who were not Jewish by origin. Before, they felt far from God and from the people of Israel. He reminds them that they now belong to God's family, together with Jewish believers. The apostles and prophets are the foundation, and Christ is the cornerstone that holds everything together.

You are not a loose stone. God joins you to other believers to form his house. Seek out a Christian community, serve with humility, and work for unity. God is still building, and you have a place in that work.
exp.4:8:
The verse says that the fruit of the Spirit, that is, what a life guided by God produces, is seen in three things: goodness, righteousness, and truth. It is in parentheses because it is a brief explanation within a longer idea. In some ancient manuscripts the phrase "fruit of the light" appears instead of "fruit of the Spirit," and scholars mention this, but the meaning is very similar.

The apostle Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus, who once lived in the darkness of paganism. He reminds them that now, through Christ, they are light, and so they must live as children of light, not joining in the works of darkness.

Today we can ask ourselves: in my work, my family, and my conversations, is goodness, righteousness, and truth evident? Choose one of the three and practice it this week, for example by being honest in some small matter where no one would see you.
exp.0:11:
This verse says that God chose us and gave us an inheritance in Christ, so that our lives would be for the praise of his glory. "Those of us who first trusted in Christ" means those who first placed our hope in him. The word "trusted" here means to rely on him with expectation.

Paul writes this letter from prison to the believers in Ephesus. By saying "we," he most likely refers to the first Jewish believers, and in the next verse he says "you," speaking to believers from other peoples. Many understand it this way, though some think "we" includes everyone. His purpose is to show that all receive the same grace.

For today: your life does not revolve only around your achievements. Today you can thank God out loud and treat someone with patience and kindness. In this way your life reflects how good he is.
exp.3:26:
It says we should not give room or opportunity to the devil in our lives. "Give place" means allowing someone to gain a foothold, like leaving a door open. "Devil" is the enemy of God and of his people.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just spoken to them about leaving behind lying and not holding on to anger. Anger that is kept, just like lying, can become an open door to evil. That is why the verse sits alongside the phrase "do not let the sun go down on your anger." After that he speaks of stealing and of harmful words, other ways of giving place to evil.

Today we can apply it this way: if someone has offended you, do not hold on to resentment. Speak with that person calmly, ask for forgiveness or forgive, and try to settle the matter quickly, before the day ends.
exp.0:15:
He says that Paul does not stop giving thanks to God for the believers he is writing to. The phrase "I do not stop" means "I do not stop doing this." "You" refers to "you" in the verse. "Remembering you" means that he remembers them by name or with affection when he prays. His thanksgiving and his prayer are constant.

Paul is the one speaking, writing this letter to the Christians in Ephesus (some early manuscripts do not include "in Ephesus," so some think the letter circulated among several churches). He rejoices because he has heard of their faith in Jesus and of their love for all the believers. This verse leads into the prayer that follows, where he asks that God give them wisdom and spiritual understanding.

For today: think of someone in your church, family, or workplace, and thank God for that person. Then pray for them by name, without waiting for a problem to arise.
exp.1:17:
This verse says that, thanks to Christ ("him"), both Jews and non-Jews can come near to God the Father. We do so through one and the same Spirit, the Holy Spirit. The phrase "have access" means that we have the privilege, the permission, to come into his presence. The words "we both" refer to those two groups.

Paul writes to Christians of non-Jewish background in Ephesus. Before this verse he explains that Christ, through the cross, ended the hostility between Jews and non-Jews and reconciled them to God in one body. Afterward he says they are no longer strangers, but members of God's family. His purpose is to show them that they fully belong.

For today: you can approach God with confidence, without feeling unworthy or second-class. Pray simply, knowing that Christ opened the way. And receive other believers warmly, even if they are very different from you, because they come to the same Father.
exp.3:18:
They say that some people came to lose the sensitivity of their conscience, that is, that inner voice that warns us when something is wrong. By no longer feeling it, they gave themselves over to lasciviousness (living without shame or limits) and pursued with greediness (with great eagerness and no control) every kind of uncleanness.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus, who were mostly not Jews. He urges them firmly not to live as they once did, when their minds were dark and far from God. Then he reminds them that they learned Christ in a different way, and that changes everything.

For today: do not ignore the warnings of your conscience, because hardening it step by step costs dearly. Ask God for a sensitive heart, and when something troubles you, listen to it, confess it, and correct your course with humility.
exp.5:9:
Paul tells the believers: "Finally," that is, to finish the letter, be strengthened in the Lord. "Be strong" means "take strength," and "the power of his might" speaks of the great power that comes from God. The strength is not our own; it is received by being united to Christ.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus, and many believe he wrote it while he was in prison. He has just given advice about life at home and at work, speaking to servants and masters. With this verse he begins his closing: the Christian life also faces a spiritual struggle, and that is why we need the strength of God, not our own.

When you feel tired or weak in the face of a trial, do not rely only on your own effort. Ask God for strength, pray, and seek his Word before facing the day.
exp.1:5:
He says that God raised us up together with Christ and gave us a place with Him in the heavenly places. The verse's word "together" means "at the same time" or "united with Christ." "Made us sit" speaks of a place of honor and rest. Paul presents this as something already accomplished, even though we still live on earth.

Paul is writing to the believers in Ephesus. Earlier he reminded them that they were spiritually dead in their sins. Now he explains that God, out of His mercy and love, gave them new life. All of this is by grace, not by their own merit, as the following verses say. Some understand the "sitting in the heavenly places" as a present spiritual position, and others as a promise that will be fully seen later.

For today: if you are united with Christ, your worth does not depend on your failures or your achievements. Live with gratitude and confidence, knowing that God has already accepted you in Christ.
exp.5:11:
It says our deepest battle is not against other people ("flesh and blood"), but against evil spiritual forces. "Principalities" and "powers" are forces with authority; "rulers of the world" and "rulers of the darkness" refer to forces that dominate this dark world; "in high places" points to the spiritual realm, not to something visible.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus, probably from prison. Closing the letter, he encourages them to be strong in the Lord, not in their own strength. He explains whom they are fighting against so they will understand why they need the whole armor of God. Scholars debate how these forces are organized, but Paul insists that they are real.

Today, when someone hurts you or contradicts you, remember that this person is not your real enemy. Respond with prayer, truth, and patience, and ask God for the strength not to repay evil with evil.
exp.1:2:
It says that all of us, Jews and non-Jews alike, once lived driven by the desires of the flesh, that is, our human nature apart from God. We did what the body and the mind wanted. "Children of wrath" means that we deserved God's judgment. "By nature" indicates that this condition was ours from the beginning, just like everyone else's. Christians debate exactly how to understand this, but all acknowledge that no one escapes sin.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus. First he describes their condition, and here he includes himself with the "we." He does this to show how deep the human need was. In this way he prepares for the "But God" of the next verse, where the mercy that changes everything appears.

For today: remembering where God brought us from helps us live with humility and gratitude. Instead of judging others harshly, we can treat them with the patience God showed us.
exp.5:18:
Paul asks that they pray for him too. He wants God to give him the right words when he opens his mouth to speak, and to let him speak with confidence, that is, with courage and without fear. His aim is to make known the mystery of the gospel. In the Bible, a "mystery" is not something strange, but a plan of God that was hidden and has now been revealed in Christ.

Paul writes this letter from prison. He has just spoken of the armor of God and of constant prayer for all believers. Even though he is an apostle, he recognizes that he needs the prayers of others. Two verses later he calls himself an ambassador in chains, since his imprisonment does not put out his desire to proclaim Christ.

Today we can pray for those who preach and teach, and also ask for the courage to speak about Jesus simply and truthfully in our work, family, or school.
exp.2:3:
Paul says that, by reading what he has already written to them, the Ephesians can see how much he understands about the mystery of Christ. The word "understanding" here means comprehension or knowledge. A "mystery," in the Bible, is something that was hidden and that God now makes known.

Paul writes from prison to a church with many non-Jewish believers. He had already spoken to them briefly about this revelation. Now he invites them to read and check that his teaching comes from God. The mystery, according to the verses that follow, is that the Gentiles are also heirs together with Israel of the promises in Christ.

Today we can learn to read the Bible with attention and humility, asking God to help us understand. And seeing that Christ unites people who are very different, we can welcome with affection those who are different from us.
exp.5:17:
Paul says that we should pray at all times, with every kind of prayer and request, led by the Spirit. The old words "deprecation" and "supplication" are used for asking earnestly and humbly, and the word "watching" means being alert and awake, while "perseverance" means steady persistence. Also, we should pray for all the saints, that is, for all believers.

Paul writes from prison to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just described the armor of God, which protects us in spiritual struggle. This prayer ties together everything before it: it is not another piece of the armor, but the way of living with it. Right after, he asks them to pray for him as well, that he may speak the gospel with boldness.

For today: choose a brother or sister in your church and pray for that person this week, staying alert to what God shows you. When you think of that person during the day, offer a short prayer for them.
exp.4:25:
This verse says that Christ gave himself up for the church to set it apart for God and to cleanse it. The word "washing" here refers to a bath or cleansing with water. It speaks of a washing with water "by the word."

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus and uses Christ's love for his church as a model for husbands. About "the washing of water," some think it points to baptism, and others take it as an image of spiritual cleansing through the message of the gospel. The Bible does not explain this in more detail, so it can be understood in several ways.

For today: let the Word of God cleanse and shape you. Read it with humility and let it correct your attitudes. And if you are married, love by seeking your spouse's spiritual and personal good, not your own comfort.
exp.3:2:
What it says: Paul asks us to make a careful and earnest effort (the word "endeavouring" means making a diligent, attentive effort) to keep the unity that the Holy Spirit has already created among believers. That unity is held together by peace, as if peace were a cord that keeps us bound together.

Context: Paul writes from prison to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just asked them for humility, gentleness and patience. Then he reminds them of what they all share: one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith. Unity is not manufactured; it is looked after, because God has already given it.

For today: When you have a disagreement with someone in your church or your family, do not aim to win the argument. First seek peace: listen patiently, speak calmly, and take the first step toward reconciliation.
exp.3:19:
Paul says that the believers in Ephesus did not come to know Christ in that way; in other words, they did not learn to live like the pagans he has just described. The word "so" points to that life of impurity, hardened hearts, and dulled conscience. Learning Christ is not only receiving information but knowing Him personally and following His way.

Paul writes from prison to Christians of non-Jewish background. He has just described how the Gentiles lived without God, and now he marks the contrast. He wants to remind them that their new life in Christ must look different, and he prepares the call to put off the old self in the verses that follow.

For today: knowing Christ should change the way we live. Ask yourself today what habit or attitude does not fit with what you have learned from Jesus, and ask Him for help to let it go.
exp.0:16:
Paul prays that God, whom he calls "the God of our Lord Jesus Christ" and "the Father of glory," may give believers "the spirit of wisdom and revelation." This means a spiritual understanding for knowing God better. The phrase "may give you" means "give to them." Some think "spirit" refers to the Holy Spirit, and others to an attitude of the heart; both ideas are possible.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just thanked God for their faith and their love toward all the saints, that is, the believers. Now he asks for something more: that they keep growing in the knowledge of God. The verses that follow explain that he wants the eyes of their hearts to be enlightened so they can understand the hope and the power of God.

For today: before you read the Bible, ask God to help you know Him better. Do not only look for information, but for a deeper relationship with Him.
exp.3:15:
It says that Christ is the head, and that from him the whole body, the church, receives what it needs to live. The phrase about being put together and tied well speaks of a body that is well built and joined together. The joints are the places where the parts connect, and what each part contributes or receives is what supplies the body. Each part works according to its function. So each member, in its own measure, helps the body grow, and everything is built up in love.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus from prison. He had been speaking of the gifts Christ gave to his church, and he wanted them to stop being unstable like children who are carried off by deceptive teachings. What follows is a call to live differently from the pagans.

For today: do not remain a spectator in your church. Ask God how you can serve with what you have, even if it seems small, and do it with love.
exp.4:5:
Paul says that no one should persuade us with "empty words," that is, hollow or deceptive speeches, into thinking that certain sins are not serious. He warns that because of these things comes the wrath of God, his just judgment, upon the "children of disobedience," that is, those who live in rebellion against God.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just named sins such as sexual immorality, impurity, and greed. Some people were probably trying to downplay them. He reminds them that such a way of life does not fit with the kingdom of Christ. Then he tells them that they used to be darkness, but now they are light.

For today: do not accept without thinking the ideas that say sin is "not such a big deal." Compare what you hear, on social media, on television, or among friends, with what the Bible says, and ask God for wisdom to live as a child of light.
exp.5:7:
This verse says that God sees and rewards every good thing we do. It does not matter whether the person was a slave or free: each one will receive from the Lord the good that they did. The word "whatsoever" means "whatever," and "shall he receive of the Lord" speaks of a reward that comes from God, not from people.

The apostle Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus. Earlier he spoke to servants, that is, to slaves, and encouraged them to work with sincerity, not only when the master is watching. Then he speaks to masters, so that they treat their servants well, because all of them have one Master in heaven.

Today we can work with honesty and a good attitude, even when no one sees us or recognizes us. Do your work, your chores, or your service as for God, trusting that he sees and values every effort.
exp.5:22:
He says that Paul wishes three things for the brothers and sisters: peace, love, and faith. All of this comes from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The word "á" is the preposition "a" written in an old way, and the phrase "love with faith" can be understood as a love that goes together with trust in God.

Paul writes this letter while he is in prison, and he ends it with an affectionate farewell. He has just said that Tychicus would carry news from him to encourage the believers in Ephesus. Now he gives them a blessing. Notice that peace, love, and faith are not presented as human achievements, but as gifts that come from God.

For today: instead of striving alone to have peace or love, we can ask God for them each day. We can also wish them for others and express them to them, with a kind word or a prayer for them.
exp.5:19:
Paul says that he is an ambassador, that is, a representative sent to speak on behalf of another, and that he is one "in bonds," meaning while he is imprisoned. He asks that he may speak of the gospel "boldly," with courage and without fear, "as I ought to speak," that is, as is fitting for his calling.

Paul writes this letter from prison, probably in Rome, although some scholars think of another place. He has just asked the believers to pray for him. He does not ask to be set free, but that he may have the words and confidence to proclaim the mystery of the gospel. His imprisonment does not change his mission.

For today: even when you face fear, shame, or difficult circumstances, you can still be a witness for Christ. Pray for courage and for other believers, and speak of your faith with clarity, respect, and love.
exp.0:7:
This verse says that God's grace was not only given to us, but overflowed, that is, it abounded in us. That abundance came together with wisdom (knowing how to live according to God) and understanding (comprehension, insight). The small connecting word here is simply the "and" from before. Some understand that God poured out his grace with wisdom; others, that he gave us wisdom as part of that grace.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus, praising God for the blessings received in Christ: forgiveness, redemption, and acceptance. He then explains that God made known to them the mystery of his plan: to gather all things together in Christ.

Today we can remember that God does not give his grace sparingly. If you need to understand your life or make decisions, ask God for wisdom with confidence, knowing that he is generous and wants you to know his will.
exp.4:0:
It says that believers should resemble God, imitating his way of acting, because we are his beloved children. The word "therefore" indicates a conclusion drawn from what came before. "Be ye" means "be," and "followers" are those who copy the example of another, like a child who learns from his father.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus. Just before, he encouraged them to forgive one another as God forgave them in Christ. Then he explains that imitating God means walking in love, as Christ did, who gave himself up for us. Then he speaks of living in purity, becoming holy people, that is, those who belong to God.

Today we can ask ourselves, facing a difficult situation: "What would God do here?" Perhaps by forgiving someone, helping a person in need, or speaking with patience. We do this not to earn his love, but because we are already loved by him.
exp.4:15:
It says we should make good use of the time. "Redeeming" here means buying back or getting the greatest benefit from something valuable. "Carefully" and "evil" show that we must live with care, because the days are full of wickedness and dangers.

The apostle Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus. He has just called them to wake up from spiritual death and to walk as wise people, not as fools. Then he asks them to understand the will of the Lord and to be filled with the Spirit. Some scholars think that "redeeming the time" speaks of seizing every opportunity God gives; others, of using time well in the middle of a hostile world.

Today we can examine how we use our hours. Before filling the day with distractions, let us set aside a moment to pray, read the Bible, and do good to someone. In this way we live with purpose and wisdom.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that, before coming to know Christ, the believers in Ephesus lived by the customs and values of this world, under the influence of an evil spiritual force. The word "walked" in the verse is explained as meaning "lived." The phrase "the prince of the power of the air" is usually understood as referring to Satan, and "the children of disobedience" are those who live in rebellion against God.

Paul writes to Christians in Ephesus, most of whom were not of Jewish origin. He wants them to see the rescue God brought them from, so that they will value his grace. For this reason he describes their former condition: spiritually dead and carried along by a system opposed to God. Some scholars debate the exact meaning of "the power of the air," but almost all see in it an evil spiritual power.

For today: remembering what Christ has done for us frees us from pride and moves us to gratitude. It also invites us to examine whether we still follow the currents of the world out of habit, and to ask God to guide us.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that everything God made known through the church was not an afterthought. It was a plan settled from eternity, and it was fulfilled in Christ Jesus our Lord. "Eternal purpose" means a firm intention of God that has no beginning.

Paul writes this letter, probably from prison, to believers who were mostly not Jews. He explains that God has opened salvation to them too, and that the church, made up of people from all nations, shows God's wisdom even to spiritual beings. Scholars debate exactly who the "rulers and authorities" are, but the text says they are in the heavenly realms.

For today: your life is not adrift. If you are in Christ, you are part of a plan that God conceived in love from long ago. When everything seems uncertain, you can rest in the fact that God is still working with purpose.
exp.5:5:
The passage says that servants should not work only when someone is watching them, nor to win the approval of people. Working only under the master's eye is the idea behind the phrase "eyeservice." Instead, they should see themselves as servants of Christ, doing God's will wholeheartedly, gladly and from the heart.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus. In his time slavery was common, and he addresses servants within his instructions for life in the household. He neither approves nor explains the system here; he teaches how to live out the faith within that reality. He reminds them that their true Lord is Christ, who sees everything.

For today: work with honesty and care even when no one is supervising you. Do your job, keep your word, and treat others well, knowing that God sees and values what you do in private.
exp.4:30:
This verse says that a man leaves his father and mother to be joined to his wife, and that the two become one. The phrase "shall be joined" means he is united to her, clinging to her, staying close. "One flesh" speaks of a very deep union, not only physical but one that lasts for the whole of life.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus about how to live out marriage. Here he quotes Genesis 2:24, the account of creation. He then explains that this mystery (something God was gradually revealing) points to the union between Christ and his church. In this way, the love of marriage reflects the love of Christ.

For today: if you are married, seek to give your spouse priority through concrete actions, such as listening to them, deciding together, and caring for them. If you are about to marry, prepare to stop depending on your parents and to build a new home, while showing respect toward them.
exp.3:0:
Paul says that he is a prisoner "in the Lord," that is, imprisoned for serving Christ. From that place he urges the believers to walk, that is, to live and conduct themselves, in a way worthy of the calling God has given them. "I beseech you" means "I urge you" or "I ask you with affection."

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus. Chapters 1 through 3 speak of what God has already done for them: he saved them by grace and joined them into one people. From chapter 4 onward, Paul turns to practice: if God has called us, our lives should reflect it. The verses that follow show how: with humility, patience and love.

Today you might ask yourself: does the way I treat others, at home, in church or at work, show that God has called me? Today, choose one concrete act of patience.
exp.5:16:
It says we should take the "helmet of salvation," that is, the helmet of salvation, which protects the head. It also says we should take "the sword of the Spirit," which is the word of God. "Helmet" is the piece of armor worn on the head, and "salvation" here refers to being saved.

Paul writes this letter, probably from prison, to the believers in Ephesus. He uses the image of a Roman soldier's armor to teach them to resist the spiritual forces of evil. The sword is the only piece meant for attack, and Paul immediately speaks of praying at all times.

When doubt or temptation comes, do not rely only on your own ideas. Remember a specific promise from the Bible, learn it by heart, and repeat it in prayer. Resting in the salvation that Christ has already given you gives you firmness, and his word gives you an answer.
exp.0:3:
This verse says that God chose us in Christ before he created the world. His purpose was that we would be holy, that is, set apart for Him, and without blame, meaning without fault before Him. All of this happens "in love." Some understand that this love is God's love, and others understand it as the love with which we live.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Ephesus. He begins by praising God for the spiritual blessings He gives in Christ. He wants his readers to understand that their salvation did not begin with them, but with God's loving plan. Christians have interpreted in several ways how this choosing relates to human freedom.

For today: if God chose you with love, you do not have to earn His acceptance. Live with gratitude, seeking a clean life full of love toward others.
exp.1:13:
He says that Jesus himself is our peace. He united two groups who had been separated: Jews and non-Jews (Gentiles). The "middle wall of partition" is an image of what divided them. Many believe it refers to the barrier in the temple that kept Gentiles apart, or to the law with its rituals; the Bible uses it as a figure, not as a literal wall.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus, most of whom were not Jewish. He wants them to understand that they were once far from God and from his people, but that now, through the blood of Christ, they have been brought near. He shows them that the cross does not only reconcile them to God, but also to one another as believers.

For today: if Christ broke down the wall, let us not build it up again ourselves. This week, reach out kindly to someone from a different background, culture, or way of thinking in your church, and seek peace with that person.
exp.2:1:
It says that Paul takes for granted that the Ephesians have already heard of the grace of God that was given to him for them. The stewardship entrusted to him means a responsibility or assignment: God gave Paul the task of bringing his grace, his undeserved favor, to the non-Jews. The phrase "if indeed you have heard" does not express doubt, but reminds them of something they already know.

Paul writes from prison, and he calls himself a prisoner for Christ Jesus because his imprisonment comes from serving Christ and preaching to the Gentiles. He pauses his prayer to explain the mystery: that Jews and Gentiles form one people in Christ. His assignment was not a personal honor, but a service for them.

For today: God gives us gifts, tasks, and opportunities by grace, not for boasting, but to serve others. Ask yourself: whom can I bless with what God has entrusted to me?
exp.3:4:
It says that all believers share the same essentials: one Lord, who is Jesus Christ; one faith, that is, the trust and basic teachings of the gospel; and one baptism, the public sign that we belong to Christ. The word "eagerly" in verse 3 means "making every effort, with diligence."

Paul writes this letter, probably from prison, to the Christians in Ephesus, where Jews and non-Jews lived together. He asks them to guard the unity that the Spirit has already given them. This list of "ones" explains why they should live in peace. Christians differ in how they understand baptism, but Paul stresses that there is a common foundation.

For today: before arguing with another believer over secondary differences, remember that you both follow the same Lord. Look for one concrete way today to treat that person with peace and respect.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that God's "mystery" was not made clear to earlier generations, but now the Spirit has revealed it to Christ's apostles and prophets. A "mystery" is a plan of God that was hidden and is now made known. The word "holy" in the verse means set apart for God. The phrase "made known" appears in the verse as "revealed," which is what the older wording means.

Paul writes this letter, probably from prison, to Christians of non-Jewish background. He wants them to understand the plan of God that Christ fulfills: the Gentiles, or non-Jews, are also part of God's people. The verses that follow explain this clearly.

For today: give thanks that God makes himself known by his own initiative, not by our merit. Read the Bible asking the Spirit to help you understand it, and receive with humility and joy those who are different from you, for in Christ all of us are welcome.
exp.1:10:
This verse asks believers not to forget their past. Paul is speaking to the Gentiles, that is, to those who were not Jews. The Jews called them "uncircumcision," while the Jews themselves were called "circumcision." That circumcision was a mark made on the body by human hands. Remember means to keep something in mind.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Ephesus, which was made up largely of Gentiles. He has just said that salvation is by grace and not by works. Now he reminds them that they were once outside the people of Israel and her promises, so that they would value what Christ did in bringing them near to God.

For today: remembering where God rescued us keeps us humble and grateful. It also helps us welcome with kindness those who see faith from afar, because we too were received by pure grace.
exp.2:19:
What it says: This verse praises God and says that He is able to do far more than we ask or even imagine. "Powerful" means that He has the strength to do it. The word for "or" is simply "or," and "power" means strength. That power is already at work within believers.

Context: Paul writes this letter, and here he closes a prayer for the Christians in Ephesus. He had asked that they would know the love of Christ and be filled with God. Now he ends with praise, trusting that God can accomplish what seems too great. As many believe, Paul was writing from prison, though the verse does not say so.

For today: When you pray, do not limit God by your own calculations. Ask Him with confidence, even for great things, and remember that His power is already working in you to help you love, forgive, and persevere. He can answer in ways better than you imagine.
exp.4:23:
This verse compares the church to wives. Just as the church places itself under the care and guidance of Christ, wives are also to submit to their own husbands in every thing. The words "subject" and "submit" speak of willingly placing oneself under the direction of another.

The apostle Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus. After speaking about living in the love of Christ, he explains how that faith is lived out in the home. Next he asks husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church, giving himself for her. Christians understand in different ways how far the "in every thing" reaches, but all notice that the model of authority is the service and sacrifice of Christ.

For today: in marriage, both can practice respect and mutual service, listening to each other with humility and seeking together what pleases God.
exp.1:18:
This verse says that believers who once were far from God are no longer "strangers" (people from another country) nor "newcomers" (recent arrivals without rights). Now they are "fellow citizens" with the saints, that is, the people of God, and "members of the household of God," that is, members of his family, of his house.

Paul writes to Christians of non-Jewish background in Ephesus. Before, they were separated from the people of Israel and from God's promises. Paul reminds them that Christ brought peace and opened the way to the Father for Jews and non-Jews alike. That is why no one is second-class in the church anymore. The next verse speaks of a building where everyone fits together in Christ.

For today: if you believe in Jesus, you belong to God's family. You can pray with confidence, without feeling like an outsider. And you can also welcome warmly the person who is new to your church, making them feel at home.
exp.4:29:
It says that believers are part of Christ, just as the members of a body are part of the body. The phrase "his flesh and his bones" is a way of speaking about a very close and real union. Some ancient manuscripts do not include this phrase, but most Bibles keep it.

Paul writes to the church in Ephesus. He is speaking about how marriage should be, and he uses Christ's love for his church as an example. Just as a man cares for his own body, Christ cares for those who belong to him. The phrase sounds like Genesis 2:23, where Adam speaks about Eve. Paul himself later says that this mystery refers to Christ and the church.

For today: if you are joined to Christ, you do not walk alone. He sustains and cares for you. This invites us to treat other believers and our family with that same care, without selfishness.
exp.3:3:
It says that we believers form one body, the church, and that the same Holy Spirit lives and works in all of us. It also says that God called us to one hope. "Calling" means the call God gave us, and "hope" is the confident trust in what God has promised.

Paul writes this letter, and he most likely writes it while imprisoned. Before this, he asked for humility, gentleness, and patience to bear with one another in love. Here he gives the reason: unity is not something we invent, because it already exists since God made us one body. Then he continues with "one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God."

For today: when it is hard to get along with another believer, remember that God called them just as he called you. Today, look for one concrete act of peace, such as asking forgiveness, listening calmly, or speaking a kind word.
exp.5:8:
Paul tells the masters to treat their servants with the same spirit of goodwill and respect that is asked of the servants. "Forbearing threatening" means giving up intimidating or frightening them. "Respect of persons" means favoritism: God does not look at whether someone is a master or a servant, rich or poor. Both have the same Master in heaven.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Ephesus, in a world where slavery was common. Just before, he spoke to the servants, and now he speaks to the masters. He reminds them that they too are accountable. Without attacking the system head-on, this teaching removes the foundation of harsh treatment and of superiority.

For today: if you have authority over others, such as a boss, a parent, or a leader, avoid giving orders with fear or threats. Treat others with respect, remembering that one day you will give an account to God.
exp.5:3:
This verse tells fathers not to provoke their children to anger through harsh or unfair treatment. Instead, they should raise them with teaching and correction, following the way of the Lord. "Discipline" speaks of guiding and correcting; "admonition" means warning and advising with words.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus. Just before, he asks children to honor their parents. Now he turns to parents, so that their authority will not be abusive. Later he will speak of servants and masters, so he is showing how faith is lived out in household relationships.

For today: if you need to correct a child, do it calmly, explaining why, and without humiliating them. Make sure they feel you correct them because you love them, and that they see in you an example of Christ.
exp.0:10:
This verse says that in Christ we also have received an inheritance. Here the idea is not chance but of receiving a portion or inheritance. "Predestined" means that God planned it beforehand. Everything happens according to the purpose of God, who works all things according to the plan of his own will, that is, his wise and settled design.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus from prison. He has just spoken of God's plan to gather all things together in Christ. Now he shows that believers are part of that plan. Christians have understood predestination in different ways, but they all agree that God has a purpose and that the goal is to praise his glory.

For today: when life feels uncertain or without direction, remember that your life in Christ is not an accident. Rest in the fact that God is wise and faithful, and live with gratitude, seeking to honor him in everyday life.
exp.2:9:
It says God wants to show his wisdom, which has many facets and colors, through the church. That display is meant for the "principalities and powers in heavenly places," that is, spiritual beings and the authorities of the unseen world. "Made known" means given to be known. "Manifold" means varied, rich, with many aspects.

Paul writes from prison and speaks with humility about his calling to preach to the Gentiles. The "mystery" is that Jews and non-Jews form one people in Christ. Scholars debate whether those heavenly powers are good angels, evil spirits, or both; the text does not make this clear.

For today: when believers who are very different love and forgive one another, the church shows God's wisdom. Try this week to draw near with kindness to a brother or sister who is very different from you.
exp.4:24:
It says that husbands should love their wives in the same way that Christ loved the church. That love was not only in words: Christ gave himself up for her, that is, he gave his life. The word "love" in this verse is in an older form of the wording, so the reader will see it in the King James wording above.

The one who speaks is the apostle Paul, who writes to the believers in Ephesus. Shortly before, he spoke of mutual submission and of the wife toward her husband. Now he addresses husbands, and instead of speaking of command, he calls them to a love that serves and sacrifices. In his time, this was a very strong demand.

For today: if you are a husband, think of one concrete thing you can give up or do this week, such as time, comfort, or an opinion, to serve your wife without expecting anything in return.
exp.3:12:
It says that the gifts Christ gave to the church (apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers) continue his work until we all come to be united in the faith and in truly knowing the Son of God. "Perfect man" means a mature, complete person. The word "unto" is an older way of saying "to," and "doctors" means teachers. The goal is to be like Christ in his fullness.

Paul, imprisoned for the sake of the gospel, writes to the believers in Ephesus. He explains that Christ distributed different ministries to prepare all believers to serve and build up the body of Christ. Then he warns against deceptive teachings. Some understand "perfect man" to mean the whole church reaching maturity; others, the maturity of each believer.

For today: do not see the Christian life as something individual. Take part in your church, listen to biblical teaching, and serve with your gift. In this way you will grow in maturity and will not be carried away by just any idea.
exp.1:11:
This verse reminds believers from a non-Jewish background what their life was like before they came to know Jesus. They did not have Christ, they did not belong to the people of Israel, and they did not know the promises of God. The phrase "commonwealth of Israel" refers to the community or nation of Israel. The phrase "strangers from the covenants" means that they were outsiders to the agreements God made with his people. They lived without hope and without knowing the true God.

The apostle Paul writes to Christians of Gentile origin. He asks them to remember their past so that they will value what God has done for them. The verses that follow show the turn: now, through the blood of Christ, they are no longer far away, and Jesus broke down the wall that separated Jews and Gentiles.

For today: remember where God brought you from, not to feel shame, but to live with gratitude. And treat with love and humility those who are still "far off."
exp.5:20:
Paul tells the Ephesians that he wants them to know how he is doing and what he is up to. To that end, he lets them know that Tychicus will tell them everything. The word "affairs" here does not mean trade or business, but matters or circumstances. "How I do" means how he is. Paul calls Tychicus a dear brother and a faithful servant, that is, a trustworthy worker in the work of the Lord.

Paul writes from prison, bound in chains for preaching the gospel. Tychicus is the one carrying the letter, and he can give news in person. Paul also sends him to encourage the believers, as the next verse says. As for where Paul was imprisoned, tradition suggests Rome, though some scholars propose other places.

God uses faithful and humble people, like Tychicus, to encourage others. Today we can do something similar: call, visit, or write to someone who is going through a hard time, to give them encouragement and companionship. And if you are going through a trial, let your brothers and sisters know how you are doing, so they can pray for you.
exp.4:1:
It says that we should live each day in love, following the example of Christ. He loved us so much that he gave himself up for us. The words "offering and sacrifice" recall the offerings of the Old Testament, and "sweet-smelling" is a way of saying that God received it with pleasure.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just asked them to imitate God as beloved children. Then he warns them against immorality, greed, and crude speech. Thus the love of Christ is the model for the whole new life of the believer.

Today we can ask ourselves: "How would Jesus love in this situation?" Perhaps it means forgiving someone, giving time to a tired family member, or serving without expecting applause. Christian love shows itself in practical self-giving, not only in words.
exp.4:9:
This verse invites us to prove, that is, to examine and test, what things are pleasing to the Lord. The word "proving" here does not simply mean saying "it is fine," but testing carefully, like someone who checks something to be sure. What is pleasing to God is the goal that guides our way of living.

The apostle Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus. He reminds them that before they lived in darkness, without knowing God, but now they are light in the Lord. For this reason he asks them to walk as children of light, and he explains that the fruit of that light is goodness, righteousness and truth. Proving what is pleasing to the Lord is part of that new life.

Today, before making a decision, whether at work, in a friendship or in how we use our time, we can ask ourselves sincerely: "Is this pleasing to the Lord?" Praying and seeking his Word helps us answer with wisdom.
exp.5:6:
It says we should work or serve with willingness and from the heart, "with good will," as if we were doing the work for the Lord himself and not only for people. The idea is that God is the one who truly sees and values what we do.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus. In this passage he speaks to servants or slaves, which was common in the Roman world of his time. He does not approve or defend slavery here; rather, he gives them a new reason for their conduct: serving Christ. Then, in the verses that follow, he also urges masters to treat their servants well, since God shows no partiality.

Today we can apply this at work, in our studies, or at home. Do your tasks with honesty and a good attitude, even when no one sees you or thanks you, remembering that at heart you do them for God.
exp.3:1:
This verse describes how the life of a believer should be: with humility, which means not thinking of yourself as better than others; with meekness, which means gentle and non-violent treatment; and with patience, which means bearing with others in love. Bearing with others means tolerating their faults without giving up.

Paul writes from prison ("a prisoner in the Lord") to the Christians of Ephesus, who were Jews and Gentiles together. He asks them to live in a way worthy of their calling. These attitudes prepare the way for caring for the unity of the Spirit in the church.

Today, think of a person who is hard for you to put up with, in the family, at work, or in church. Before reacting, take a breath, pray for that person, and respond with calm and kindness. Loving someone does not mean pretending nothing is wrong, but choosing patience.
exp.2:15:
Paul asks that God the Father would give strength to the believers. This strength reaches the inner man, that is, the deepest part of the person, and it comes through God's Spirit. God gives it according to the riches of his glory, that is, according to how much he has, not according to how little we deserve.

Paul writes from prison to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just explained that Jews and non-Jews form one people in Christ. Now he kneels and prays for them. His prayer leads to the next step: that Christ would dwell in their hearts through faith and that they would know the love of God.

For today: when you feel tired on the inside, do not rely only on your own willpower. Ask the Father that his Spirit would strengthen you, and trust that he gives generously.
exp.1:4:
What it says: Paul affirms that, although we were spiritually dead because of our sins, God made us alive together with Christ. Salvation is not earned; it is a gift of grace, that is, of God's undeserved favor.

Context: Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus. Earlier he reminded them how they used to live: following their desires and far from God. Then comes the key turn: "But God," who, moved by his mercy and love, acted when no one could help themselves. Paul then explains that this new life continues with the resurrection and a place with Christ.

For today: When you feel unworthy or weary of your failures, remember that your worth before God does not depend on your effort. Receive his forgiveness with gratitude and live for him, not to earn his love.
exp.3:31:
It says we should treat one another with kindness and compassion, and forgive one another, just as God forgave us through Christ. Kind and good-natured is the sense of the word that refers to kindness, and tenderhearted is the sense of the word that refers to feeling the pain of others.

The apostle Paul writes this in a letter to the believers in Ephesus. Just before, he had asked them not to grieve the Holy Spirit and to put away bitterness, anger, shouting, and hurtful words. This verse shows the other side: not only to leave behind what is wrong, but to practice what is good. The model and the reason for forgiveness is the forgiveness God has already given us.

Today: if someone has offended you, decide to forgive them, even if your feelings take time to catch up. You can start by praying for that person and answering them with kind treatment, remembering how much you have been forgiven yourself.
exp.5:10:
It says we should put on the whole armor that God gives us, so that we can stand firm against the devil's deceptions. The words "put on" mean the same as "clothe yourselves," and "schemes" are traps or cunning plans meant to make us fall.

The speaker is the apostle Paul, writing to the believers in Ephesus. Earlier in the letter he spoke about how to live in the family and at work, and now he closes the letter by reminding them that the Christian life also involves a spiritual struggle. First he tells them to be strengthened in the Lord, not in their own strength.

Today, before we face the day, we can pray and lean on God: trust in his truth, in his forgiveness, and in his Word. We are not alone, and we do not depend on our own strength, but on the strength that he gives us.
exp.1:19:
This verse says that believers are like a house that God is building. The foundation is the apostles and prophets, that is, their teaching and testimony. The "cornerstone" is the main stone at a corner, the one that aligns and supports the whole building. That stone is Jesus Christ himself.

Paul is writing to Christians in Ephesus, many of whom were not Jews. He reminds them that they are no longer outsiders or newcomers (people from outside or recently arrived), but part of God's family. There are different opinions about whether the prophets refers to those of the Old Testament or to those of the early church; both views are held. In any case, Christ is the center.

For today: review what you are building your life and your faith on. Read the Bible and ask God to make Jesus your point of reference in your decisions. And remember that you are not alone: you are part of a greater building, the church.
exp.1:6:
This verse says that God saved us with a purpose: that in the ages to come everyone may see how great and abundant his grace is. Grace is the favor God gives without our having earned it. His kindness toward us shows his gentle and generous way of dealing with us. All of this comes through Christ Jesus, that is, by means of him. The ages to come can refer to the coming ages, and even to eternity.
