The apostle Paul is writing to the believers in Ephesus. Earlier he reminded them that they were spiritually dead, but God gave them life together with Christ. Now he explains the reason: that their salvation be a testimony to God's grace. The next verse makes clear that salvation is a gift received through faith, not by works.

Today, when you feel unworthy or tired of failing, remember that your life is a demonstration of God's grace. Receive it with humility and gratitude, and treat others with that same kindness.
exp.3:27:
It says that the person who used to steal must stop doing so completely. Instead of taking what belongs to others, they must now work with their own hands at something honest. The verb "to steal" is the word the verse uses for stealing, and the phrase about having a need is simply the verse's idea of being in need. Work is no longer only for survival but also to have something to share.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus, who came from a pagan way of life. In this passage he explains what the new life in Christ looks like: leaving behind lying, anger that gives room to evil, and harmful words. Changing one's behavior is part of following Jesus.

Today we might ask ourselves whether there is something we take without right, such as time, money, or someone else's credit. Let us decide to work with honesty and, according to our means, to share with someone who is in need.
exp.2:2:
Here Paul explains how he came to know the "mystery." He says that he did not discover it through his own study or learn it from other people, but that God himself revealed it to him. "Was made known to me" is the meaning of the phrase "fué declarado." The phrase "as I wrote afore in few words" indicates that he had already mentioned this, in a brief summary, probably in this same letter (chapters 1 and 2). Some think it could refer to another letter, but this is not known for certain.

Paul writes from prison, and he calls himself a prisoner of Christ for the sake of the Gentiles, that is, the non-Jews. He wants them to understand that God includes them in his plan of salvation together with Israel. That is the mystery: something hidden before, which God now makes clear.

Today, we can remember that knowing God is a gift of his grace, not an achievement of our own. For this reason, when we read the Bible, it is good to humbly ask him to open our understanding.
exp.2:6:
Paul says that he was made a "minister," that is, a servant or attendant, of the gospel. This did not come from his own merit but from "the gift of the grace of God," an undeserved gift. And everything happens "according to the effectual working of his power," that is, in line with the work of God's power in him.

Paul writes this letter from prison. He has just explained the mystery: that the Gentiles, those who were not Jews, can now be heirs together with Israel in Christ. Right after this he calls himself "less than the least of all saints," which shows his humility. He does not present himself as someone great, but as someone who received an assignment.

Today, if God has given you some task or service, do not rely only on your own strength or consider yourself superior. Serve with humility and ask him for his power, because what God gives, he also sustains.
exp.4:11:
This verse says that it is shameful, even disgraceful, even just to mention what some people do in secret. "Shameful thing" means something embarrassing or dishonorable. "In secret" means done hidden from view.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus. He asks them not to take part in the works of darkness, that is, a life without God, but instead to expose them through a clean life. Some understand that "expose" means correcting with words, and others understand it as making them evident through a good example. Here he warns that there is no need to describe evil in detail in order to reject it.

Today we can be careful about what we tell, what we look at, and what we comment on. We can speak truthfully about sin when it is necessary, but without a morbid interest or gossip, and by showing the light of Christ more clearly through an honest life.
exp.4:22:
It says that the husband is the "head" of the wife, in the same way that Christ is the head of the church. It adds that Christ is the one who "gives health to the body," that is, the Savior of the church. "Health" here means salvation or rescue. "Submit" means to yield to someone or to place oneself under someone's care.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus. The passage begins by asking that everyone submit to one another out of reverence for God. Then it speaks to wives, and right after that it asks husbands to love as Christ did, who gave himself up for his church. Scholars debate whether "head" means authority, source, or both, but the context shows a leadership of service and sacrifice.

For today: if you are a husband, measure your role by Christ's self-giving, not by command. Seek to serve, listen, and care for your wife before insisting on your own way.
exp.3:14:
It says that, instead of being carried away by any false teaching, we should live according to the truth, but always with love. In this way we grow up in all things, becoming more like Christ, who is the head of the church.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Ephesus (some early manuscripts do not include "in Ephesus," and this is debated). Earlier he spoke of children tossed about by every wind of doctrine. His concern is that the church matures and stays united, like a body that grows well coordinated under its head.

For today: when you have to correct someone or defend what you believe, do it with truth and with love at the same time. Before you speak, ask yourself whether your words help that person grow or only aim to win an argument.
exp.2:14:
This verse says that the whole "family," that is, every household or lineage, takes its name from the Father. "Heaven and earth" suggests that this family includes believers living today and those who have already died. Some also understand angels to be included; the text does not make this entirely clear. In the original language there is a wordplay between "Father" and "family" that is lost in translation.

Paul writes from prison and asks the Ephesians not to lose heart because of his sufferings. He bends his knees in prayer to the Father. Earlier he has explained that Jews and non-Jews form one people in Christ, and now he prays that they will live out that unity with spiritual strength.

For today: if God is the Father of his whole family, you are not alone in your faith. Pray for other believers, even those who are different from you, and treat them as brothers and sisters.
exp.0:21:
It says that God put all things under the feet of Christ, that is, under his authority. Also, he gave him as head over all things to the church.

Here the apostle Paul speaks in a letter to the Christians in Ephesus. Before this verse, he prays that they may know the power of God, the same power that raised Jesus and seated him at his right hand. Paul wants to encourage them to see that Christ holds the highest place, above any power, and that they belong to him.

For today: when you feel fear or pressure over what you cannot control, remember that Jesus reigns over all. Pray with confidence and remain united with his church, where he sustains and accompanies you.
exp.3:5:
This verse says there is one God, and that he is the Father of all believers. He is "above all things" (he rules with authority), he acts "through all things" (he works through everything), and he is "in you all" (he lives among his people). The phrase "you all" in the old wording was a plural form meaning "all of you," and the verse as you read it addresses the whole group together.

Paul writes to the Christians of Ephesus, where believing Jews and non-Jews lived side by side. Just before this verse he lists seven "ones": body, Spirit, hope, Lord, faith, baptism, and God. He wants them to protect the unity of the church. Some think "all" refers only to believers, others that it covers all of creation; the context favors the first view.

Today we can remember that someone who thinks differently about secondary matters, but trusts in Christ, has the same Father as we do. This week, seek to approach a fellow believer with whom you have differences with respect and kindness.
exp.3:10:
This verse says that Christ himself gave different gifts to his church: people with special roles. Some were apostles (people sent out with authority), others prophets (who spoke on God's behalf), others evangelists (who announced the good news), and others pastors and teachers, that is, teachers who care for and instruct the people.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just said that Christ descended and then rose to heaven in victory. Now he explains that from there, Christ looks after his church by giving it people who strengthen it. The verses that follow say that their purpose is to prepare the saints to serve and to help the body of Christ grow.

For today: thank those whom God uses to teach and care for you, and ask him how you can serve with what you have received, without waiting for a title.
exp.1:3:
This verse marks a very important turn. "But" introduces a contrast. After describing the wrongness of our past life, Paul says that God acted. He is "rich in mercy," meaning he has compassion in abundance. He did it "for his great love wherewith he loved us," a great and real love, given even though we did not deserve it.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians of Ephesus. Earlier he reminded them that they were spiritually dead, following their own desires and the currents of this world. Now he wants to show them that their salvation did not come from their own efforts, but from the heart of God. The thought continues in the following verses: God gave us life with Christ.

Today, when you feel unworthy because of your mistakes, remember that God seeks you out out of love, not because of your merits. Respond with gratitude, accepting his forgiveness and showing others the same mercy.
exp.3:30:
This verse asks us to remove six harmful things from our lives: bitterness (resentment that is held onto), anger (feelings of irritation), wrath (fury that bursts out), clamour (shouting), evil speaking (speaking badly of others, insulting), and all malice (the desire to hurt someone). "Be put away" means we should take them completely out of our lives.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just spoken about watching our words and not grieving the Holy Spirit. These attitudes grieve the Spirit and harm the unity of the church. Then he tells them to be kind and forgiving, as God forgave them in Christ.

Today, if someone hurt you and you keep dwelling on that pain, ask God for help letting it go. Before you answer with shouting or mockery, breathe, pray, and choose a kind word. Forgiveness is the best remedy against bitterness.
exp.3:13:
It says that God wants believers to stop being like immature children, who doubt and change their opinions all the time. The phrase about being "tossed to and fro" means they are moved back and forth like waves. "Cunning plan" describes a crafty scheme, and "tricks of deception" refers to tactics that make what is false look true. The image is that of a ship without a rudder, pushed by every wind of teaching.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Ephesus. He has just explained that Christ gave various gifts to the church so that everyone would grow up in faith and in the knowledge of Jesus. For that reason, his concern is that we not become easy prey for those who teach falsehoods. He then says that the solution is to hold to the truth in love and grow in Christ.

Today, before accepting a new teaching, compare it with what the Bible says. Read the Scriptures regularly and nurture your faith together with other mature believers.
exp.5:1:
Paul says that children should honour their father and mother. To "honour" means to respect, value, and treat with esteem. Paul calls this commandment "the first with promise" because it comes from the fifth of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:12), which includes a promise. Some think "first" refers to the order, others to its importance.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus, and he does so from prison. In this part of the letter he teaches how to live out faith within the family. First he addresses the children, and then he asks the parents not to provoke them, but to raise them with love and respect for the Lord.

Today we can honour our parents by listening to them with respect, thanking them, and caring for them as they grow old. If there were wounds, honouring them does not mean accepting mistreatment, but treating them with dignity and seeking wisdom.
exp.2:7:
Paul says that he is less than the least of all believers. Even so, God gave him grace, that is, a gift he did not deserve, to proclaim the good news to the non-Jews. That good news speaks of the riches of Christ, that is, riches so great that they cannot be measured or exhausted. "Gentiles" are the peoples who were not Jews.

Paul writes this letter, probably from prison. He has just explained that the non-Jews now belong to the same people of God and receive the same promises. He calls himself humble, perhaps remembering his past as a persecutor of the church. His calling was not by his own merit, but by the grace of God.

For today: if God entrusts you with something, do not do it out of pride, and do not hold back because you feel small. Serve with humility, trusting that his grace sustains you, and share the riches of Christ with others.
exp.1:9:
This verse says that we are God's workmanship, that is, his work, something he made with care. "Created in Christ Jesus" means that God gave us a new life through Christ. We were made for good works, which God prepared beforehand, so that we would live doing them.

Paul is writing to Christians who were not of Jewish origin. He has just explained that salvation is a gift from God, not a payment for merit. Now he makes clear that good works are not the means of being saved, but the result of having been saved. Next he will remind them of how they lived before, far from God and his promises.

For today: you do not need to earn God's love. Ask him to show you one specific good action for this week, such as helping a neighbor or encouraging someone, and do it with gratitude, not out of obligation.
exp.0:20:
This verse says that Christ is placed far above every power that exists. "Principality, power, might, and dominion" are old-fashioned words for authorities and rulers, and many understand them to include both human and spiritual powers. "Every name that is named" means any title or rank one can imagine.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus and prays that they will know the great power of God. That same power raised Christ and seated him at God's right hand. Paul wants to encourage them to see that this power also works on their behalf. He then says that Christ is the head of the church.

For today: when you feel afraid in the face of problems, injustice, or forces that seem bigger than you, remember that Christ is above all of them. Pray with confidence and keep obeying him, knowing that you are not alone.
exp.3:23:
What it says: Paul invites believers to "put on" a new way of being, like someone putting on clean clothes. This "new man" is the new life that God creates in the believer. "Created after God" means made in the likeness of God. "Righteousness" means living uprightly, and "true holiness" means a life set apart for God, genuine and sincere.

Context: Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus, many of whom came from a pagan background. He reminds them that, having come to know Christ, they must no longer live as they did before. First he speaks of putting off the old self, then of renewing the mind, and then of putting on the new. Right after, he gives concrete examples: speaking the truth and handling anger well.

For today: Each morning you can ask God to help you clothe yourself in a new attitude. Choose one specific area, such as honesty in what you say, and practice it today with God's help.
exp.5:21:
Paul says he sent Tychicus to the believers in Ephesus for a clear purpose: so that they would know how Paul and his companions were doing, and so that their hearts would be encouraged. Where the verse says the phrase means "what concerns us," that is, Paul's news, the comment is removed here; the verse itself speaks of "our affairs," meaning Paul's news. The word translated here as "comfort" means to encourage and strengthen.

Paul writes from prison, describing himself as an ambassador in chains. He knows the Ephesians are concerned for him, so he sends Tychicus, whom he calls a beloved brother and a faithful minister. Tychicus carries the letter and also tells them in person how Paul is doing. Some scholars think the letter may have circulated among several churches, but the text does not confirm this.

Today, God often comforts through people. Think of someone going through a hard time and reach out to them with a phone call, a visit, or a sincere message. Your faithful presence may be the comfort God uses.
exp.4:26:
It says that Christ wants to present his church to himself full of glory, that is, beautiful and worthy of honor. He wants her to have no stain, no blemish, and nothing of the kind. His goal is for her to be holy, set apart for God, and without fault. The phrase about presenting her to himself refers to presenting the church to himself, as in a wedding.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus. He is teaching husbands to love their wives, and he uses the love of Christ as the model: Christ gave himself up for his church to cleanse her and make her his own. Paul compares marriage to the relationship between Christ and his people.

For today: if you feel stained by your failings, remember that Christ cleanses you and transforms you with love. And if you are married, seek to love with devotion and care, looking for the good of your spouse.
exp.0:8:
God made known to us the secret of his plan, meaning something that had been hidden and that he chose to reveal. His good pleasure, his kind intention and delight, shows that this plan did not come from any pressure. God had planned it by his own initiative and with joy.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Ephesus. He has been speaking about the blessings we have in Christ: being chosen, redeemed, and forgiven. Now he explains that God not only saved us but also showed us his final plan, which the next verse sums up: gathering all things together in Christ.

For today: when life feels confusing or disorderly, remember that God has a good purpose and that he does not hide it from those who trust in Christ. You can rest in his plan, read his Word carefully, and ask him for understanding, knowing that he acts with love and not with anger.
exp.4:14:
It says we should pay close attention to how we live. "Look" means "take heed," and "carefully" means with care and prudence, and "foolish" refers to those who live without thinking about the consequences. We are called to live as wise people, not as careless ones.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just spoken of the light of Christ that awakens the one who is spiritually asleep. Now he tells them that, having received that light, their way of living must show it. Right after, he adds that they should make the most of the time and seek to understand the will of the Lord.

Today we can pause before deciding how to use our time, money, and words. A good practice is to pray each morning, "Lord, teach me to live wisely today," and then ask ourselves which decision would please God most.
exp.0:19:
This verse says that the same great power of God, which Paul has been speaking about, was displayed in Christ when God raised him from the dead. Then God seated him at his own right hand, that is, at his side on the right, the place of highest honor and authority. The phrase "in the heavenly places" shows that this place is spiritual and supreme.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus and prays that they will understand the hope and the power God has given them. To show how great that power is, he compares it with what God did in Jesus: raising him up and exalting him above every authority, as the next verse goes on to say.

For today: when you feel weak, tired, or without a way out, remember that the God who raised Christ from death is the same God who works on behalf of those who believe. Ask him for strength and confidence, and rest in the fact that Jesus reigns.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that Jesus came and announced peace to everyone. "You who were far off" refers to the Gentiles, that is, those who were not part of the people of Israel. "Those who were near" are the Jews, who had received God's law and promises. The word "preached" means that he proclaimed good news.

The writer is the apostle Paul, addressing believers in Ephesus, most of whom were of Gentile origin. Before this verse, he explains that through the cross, Christ tore down the hostility between Jews and Gentiles and reconciled them to God. Paul wants his readers to understand that they now form one family, regardless of their origin.

Today we can remember that the peace of Christ is for everyone, without exception. If there is someone from whom we feel distant because of differences in culture, church, or customs, we can take a step toward reconciliation, for Christ has already opened the way.
exp.0:9:
This verse says that God has a plan: to gather all things together in Christ. The phrase "in the administration" refers to the order or arrangement that God manages, and "the fullness of the times" is the moment God himself chose. "Those in heaven and those on earth" covers everything that has been created. The idea is that Christ will be the center who unites all things.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus. Earlier he spoke of the blessing of being chosen and forgiven. Now he explains that God made known to them his plan, a purpose that had been hidden before and that he decided on from the beginning. Paul wants them to understand that their lives are part of a greater purpose.

For today: when the world or your life feels disorderly, remember that God has not lost control. You can place your worries in Christ's hands and trust that he leads everything toward his goal.
exp.5:13:
Paul says that we should stand firm, without giving in. First he speaks of having our loins girded with truth: in that time people wore long robes and fastened them with a belt so they could move about and fight. Then he speaks of the "cota de justicia," which was a coat of mail or breastplate that protected the chest and the heart.

Paul writes this letter from prison to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just said that the struggle is not against people, but against spiritual forces of evil. He uses the image of a Roman soldier to show that God gives us what we need to resist. Some think the righteousness here is the kind God gives through faith, and others think it also includes an upright life; many see both.

For today: be sincere with yourself and with others, and try to live with integrity. When truth and an upright life sustain your heart, it is harder for lies or guilt to knock you down.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that if Christ "went up," it is because he had first "come down" into the lowest parts of the earth. In other words, his ascent implies an earlier descent. The word translated as "teachers" in the older text is rendered here in modern wording, and the word "gave" appears in its usual form.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus and quotes Psalm 68:18 to show that Christ, now exalted, distributes gifts to his church. This parenthetical phrase explains that quotation. It is understood in several ways: the incarnation and Christ's humiliation even to the cross, his descent into the tomb, or the coming of the Spirit. Many believers see here his humility in becoming a man and dying.

For today: Christ's path to glory passed through humility and service. If he came down out of love, we can serve in the church with humility, using our gifts without seeking prestige, and trusting that God is the one who lifts up.
exp.3:29:
It says not to grieve the Holy Spirit. "Grieve" means to cause sorrow or pain. The Holy Spirit lives in the believer and is like a seal from God, a mark that we belong to him. That seal assures us until "the day of redemption," the moment when God will complete our salvation.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus. Shortly before, he speaks about giving up stealing, deceit, and harmful words. Right after, he mentions bitterness, anger, and shouting. In other words, the Spirit is grieved when we live in wickedness and with words that hurt others.

For today: before speaking in anger or holding on to resentment, remember that the Holy Spirit is present. Ask him for help to speak with kindness and to forgive, as God forgave you in Christ.
exp.2:11:
This verse says that, through Christ, believers have boldness, that is, freedom to speak and draw near to God without fear. "Access" means entrance: the door is open. "Confidence" is firm courage, without shame. All of this comes "by his faith," that is, by trusting in Christ, and not by our own merits.

The apostle Paul speaks, writing from prison. He has just explained that God, according to his eternal plan in Christ, shows his wisdom through the church. Then he encourages the readers not to lose heart over their sufferings, and he begins to pray for them.

For today: when you feel unworthy or guilty, do not turn away from God. Pray sincerely today, remembering that Christ has opened the door for you and that God receives you as a child, not as a stranger.
exp.2:20:
It says that glory be given to God, that is, honor and praise, both in the church and through Christ Jesus. This will be so in all generations, forever. "World without end" is an old way of saying "forever." "Amen" means "so be it."

The apostle Paul writes this letter, and here he ends a prayer for the believers in Ephesus. He asked that they know the love of Christ and be filled with God. Then he reminds them that God can do far more than we ask or imagine, and so he closes with praise. It is the end of the first half of the letter.

Today we can turn our requests into praise. Before asking something of God, or after doing so, stop to thank him for who he is. If the church lives this way, united and thankful, its very life gives glory to God.
exp.3:24:
It says that, since believers have already put away lying, they must now speak the truth to one another. The reason is that "we are members of one another," that is, parts of the same body. "Neighbour" is the person who is near us, and "speak" is the word used for speaking.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Ephesus. Earlier he told them to put off the old life and to clothe themselves with the new self, created according to God in righteousness and true holiness. Here he gives a first practical example: honesty. Afterward he goes on to speak about anger, so that it does not give the devil an opportunity.

Today we can apply this by being sincere and kind in small things: not exaggerating, not hiding the truth, and not making up false excuses. If we realize we have been lying, the best thing is to correct it soon and with humility, because trust protects the unity of the family, the church, and friends.
exp.4:6:
He says we should not be "partakers" with them. A partaker is a partner or companion who shares in a business and its profits. "Them" refers to people who live in immorality, impurity, and greed, and who deceive with empty words. In other words: do not join with them in what they do.

Paul is writing to the believers in Ephesus. He has just warned that whoever lives in these practices has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ, and that the wrath of God falls on the disobedient. His concern is that the church not be carried along by speech that makes sin seem ordinary. Then he reminds them that they once were darkness, but now they are light.

For today: we can treat all people with respect and love, but it is wise to examine our partnerships, business dealings, jokes, and customs. If anything pushes us to live against what Christ teaches, it is wise to step away with humility and firmness.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that God, before he created the world, lovingly decided that we would be his adopted children through Jesus Christ. "Chosen beforehand" means that God planned it in advance. "By the good pleasure of his will" means that he did it because he wanted to, gladly and with goodwill. "Unto himself" means that he adopts us into his own family.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus and begins with praise to God for the blessings received in Christ. In this passage he speaks of how God chose us and brought us near to himself. Christians have understood God's choosing in different ways, but all agree that salvation springs from God's initiative and goodness.

For today: if you doubt your worth or feel that you do not belong, remember that God wanted you in his family out of love, not because of your merits. Today you can pray and thank him for being his son or daughter.
exp.4:10:
He says we should not take part in or be accomplices to the evil actions that produce nothing good, the "works of darkness." Where the text says "have no fellowship," it means "do not join in" or "do not have a share in." The word "reprove" means to show them up for what they are, to expose them, or to make clear that they are wrong.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus, who once lived in the darkness of sin and are now light "in the Lord" (verse 8). Earlier he speaks of the fruit of the Spirit: goodness, righteousness and truth. He asks them to live differently from those around them. The verses that follow explain that light uncovers what was hidden.

For today: do not go along with the crowd when it comes to gossip, deceit or injustice. With respect and love, live honestly, and when it is fitting, speak the truth with gentleness. Your good example is already a light.
exp.4:7:
He says that before they came to know Christ, the believers in Ephesus were not only living in darkness, but were themselves darkness, meaning their lives were marked by sin. Now, united with the Lord, they are light. That is why they are called to walk, that is, to live each day as children of light.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Ephesus, most of whom came from a pagan background. He has just warned them not to be deceived by those who make light of sin. His point is that the new identity God has given them should be evident in their conduct. The next verse explains that the light produces goodness, righteousness and truth.

For today: think of a habit or environment where the way you act does not reflect what God has done in you. Take one concrete step today, such as being honest in something small or stepping away from a harmful conversation, trusting that Christ gives you the light to do it.
exp.3:7:
He says that Christ went up on high like a victorious king and led captivity captive, that is, he defeated the enemy powers that had people bound. Then he gave gifts to people. The sentence quoting the old spelling of "gave" and the accent mark on "á" is removed, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus and quotes Psalm 68:18, applying it to Christ. The psalm speaks of a king who returns victorious and distributes gifts. Paul uses it to show that Christ, exalted, gives each member of the church a gift for serving. Some explain "captivity" as the defeated enemies; others as the believers who have been set free. Both ideas fit the context.

Today, do not think that you have nothing to contribute. Ask God to show you the gift Christ has given you and use it with humility to help others in your church or family.
exp.1:0:
Paul tells the believers in Ephesus that they were dead in their trespasses and sins. It is a spiritual death: they lived without life before God, even though they walked around and breathed.

A note: in this older version the verse includes a phrase that is not in the original Greek. Modern translations simply say: "And he made you alive, you who were dead." Even so, the idea is clear: life comes from God.

Paul writes from prison to a church made up of Gentiles and Jews. He wants them to understand where God rescued them from, so that they can see his grace more clearly. Before speaking about salvation, he describes how serious the problem is.

Today: remember that your life with God is a gift, not an achievement of your own. That keeps us from pride and makes us more compassionate toward those who do not yet know Christ.
exp.3:28:
It says that no "corrupt" words should come out of our mouths, meaning words that are bad, rotten, or harmful. Instead, our words should be good and help build up the lives of others, so that those who hear us receive something of kindness, or "grace."

Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus, teaching them how to live as the new people that Christ is forming. Earlier he speaks of not giving room to the devil and of working honestly so that they can help others. Then he warns that bitter words grieve the Holy Spirit. In this way, the way we speak is part of the Christian life, not a minor detail.

Today, before you answer or post something, you can ask yourself: "Does this help the one who hears or reads it?" If it does not help, it is better to stay silent or to say it with kindness.
exp.1:8:
This verse says that salvation is not earned by our works, that is, by what we do to deserve it. The reason is clear: in this way no one could take pride in themselves or feel superior. The word "boast" means to show off or be proud of oneself.

The apostle Paul writes to the believers in Ephesus, many of whom were not Jews. He has just explained that salvation is a gift from God, received through faith. Right after, he makes clear that God made us for good works. In other words, works are not the root of salvation but its fruit. Thus Paul joins grace with a life that serves others.

Today, if you feel unworthy or, on the other hand, somewhat proud of your spiritual life, remember that everything is a gift. Give thanks to God in prayer and help someone this week, not to earn his love, but as a grateful response.
exp.4:21:
It says that wives should place themselves under their own husbands, in the same way they place themselves under the Lord. Submitting means putting yourself under someone's authority willingly. Wives refers to women who are married.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus. The verse before asks everyone to submit to one another out of reverence for God, so this command grows out of that shared attitude. Then Paul compares marriage with Christ and the church: the husband is the head, but Christ is the model of love and self-giving. Christians understand this submission in different ways, and it is worth reading it together with the command to husbands to love as Christ loved.

Today, we can live out this verse through mutual humility in the home: listening, respecting, and deciding together, seeking to please Christ in the relationship.
exp.0:0:
Paul presents himself as an apostle, that is, one sent out by Jesus Christ, and says he is one by the will of God, not by his own decision. He writes to the "saints" and "the faithful" (the wording "saints and faithful" appears in the verse as "saints" and "faithful"). "Saints" are the believers set apart for God, and "the faithful" are those who trust in him. All of them are "in Christ Jesus."

Paul is the one speaking, and he writes a letter to the Christians of Ephesus. Some ancient manuscripts do not include "at Ephesus," so some think the letter circulated among several churches. Paul writes to remind them who they are in Christ and to encourage them in their faith.

For today: your worth does not depend on your achievements, but on being in Christ. If you are a believer, God already calls you his own. Live today with that identity, grateful and secure.
exp.3:11:
This verse explains why Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers to the church. They had three purposes: the perfecting of the saints, meaning that believers be prepared and matured; the work of the ministry, meaning service to others; and the edifying of the body of Christ, which means strengthening the church. "Saints" refers to all believers, not only to special people.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just spoken about the unity of the church and the gifts that Christ gives. Some scholars understand that the leaders prepare everyone to serve; others read the phrase differently, but the central idea is the same: the church grows when everyone takes part.

For today: do not think that serving is only the pastor's task. Ask God what gift he has given you and use it this week to help someone in your congregation.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that Christ, through his death on the cross, reconciled both groups, Jews and non-Jews, to God and joined them together in one body. The words "both unto God" simply mean the two groups, brought together. "Having slain the enmity thereby" means that on the cross he put an end to the hostility that existed between them and also the hostility that existed toward God.

The apostle Paul writes to a church with believers of Jewish origin and believers of non-Jewish origin. Between them there was a great division over the law and its rites. Paul reminds them that Christ removed that barrier and that now all have the same access to God the Father.

For today: if Christ reconciled us all to God, there is no sense in keeping walls of pride or resentment in the church. Think of someone with whom you have distance and take a step toward peace, with a phone call, an apology, or a sincere prayer for that person.
exp.0:6:
In Christ we have "redemption," a word meaning release through the payment of a price. That price was his blood, that is, his death as a sacrifice. "Forgiveness of sins" means pardon, that our guilt is cancelled. All of this happens "according to the riches of his grace": God forgives because he is generous and kind, not because we deserve it.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Ephesus, and Christian tradition recognizes him as its author, although some scholars dispute this. He has been speaking about how God chose us and adopted us as children. Here he explains how this new relationship is possible: Christ paid for our forgiveness. He then goes on to say that God poured out his grace upon us with wisdom.

For today: when guilt weighs on you, remember that your forgiveness does not depend on your efforts, but on the grace of God. Receive it with gratitude and forgive others as well.
exp.5:4:
This verse speaks to servants, meaning the enslaved people of that time. It asks them to obey their masters "according to the flesh," that is, their human masters, with respect and seriousness, with a sincere heart, and doing it as if they were serving Christ himself.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians of Ephesus. After speaking about children and parents, he turns to another common relationship in the Roman world: that of slaves and masters. He does not approve or defend slavery here; he gives guidance for living out the faith within that reality. Then, in verse 9, he also urges masters to treat their servants well.

Today we can apply this at work: doing our tasks with honesty and a good attitude, even when no one is watching, remembering that at heart we serve the Lord.
exp.4:20:
This verse says that believers should submit to one another, or put themselves at one another's service. The word "subjected" is an old one that means "yielding" or "willing to give way." "Fear of God" does not mean fear, but respect and reverence toward Him.

The apostle Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus. He has been speaking about how to live filled with the Spirit, with praise and thanksgiving. This verse closes that teaching and opens the next one about the home. Some see it as the end of the previous sentence, and others as the beginning of the next; in both cases, mutual submission is the foundation of everything that follows.

For today: this week, look for a situation in your family, church or work where you normally want to be right, and give way with humility or serve first, doing it out of respect for God and not out of obligation.
exp.0:2:
Paul begins by praising God. "Blessed" means worthy of praise. He says that God, the Father of Jesus Christ, has already blessed us with every spiritual blessing. "Heavenly places" refers to the spiritual realm where God reigns, and "in Christ" shows that these blessings come through being united with Jesus.

Paul writes this letter to believers in Ephesus. After the greeting, he opens with a great song of praise that continues in the verses that follow: God chose us, adopted us as his children, and accepted us through his grace. Some scholars think the letter also circulated among other churches, but this is debated.

For today: before asking God for anything, begin by thanking him for what he has already given you in Christ, such as forgiveness, adoption, and hope. If you are going through a difficult time, remember that your worth and your future do not depend on your circumstances, but on what Christ has already done for you.
exp.2:8:
This verse says that Paul received the task of making everyone see how God's plan is carried out, a secret kept hidden since ancient times. The word "administration" refers to the way God manages and organizes his plan. "Mystery" is something that was hidden and that God now makes known. The word "created" is the same idea as "made." God, the Creator of all things, is the one who kept this plan and now reveals it.

Paul writes from prison to the Christians in Ephesus. He considers himself the least of the saints, yet he is grateful for the grace of preaching to the non-Jews. The mystery, according to the context of Ephesians, is that Jews and Gentiles form one body in Christ.

For today: faith is not a secret for a few. If God revealed his plan for everyone, we can share it with humility and without excluding anyone.
exp.4:31:
This verse says that the union of marriage, when Scripture speaks of leaving father and mother and becoming "one flesh," holds a "great mystery." Paul makes clear that he understands it as a picture of Christ and the church. A "mystery" is not something strange, but a hidden truth that God now makes known.

Paul writes to the Christians of Ephesus. He has just taught husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church. He quotes Genesis 2:24 and says that this ancient text points, in a deeper sense, to the union of Christ with his people. Scholars discuss some details, but the central focus is clear.

For today: live out your marriage, or your understanding of it, as a reflection of Christ's faithful love. Love with devotion, respect, and patience, and let his example guide your daily decisions.
exp.4:28:
It says that no one hates their own body. On the contrary, a person feeds and cares for it with tenderness. Paul adds that Christ does the same for the church.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus and teaches how to live the faith at home. Earlier he spoke of how Christ loved the church and gave himself for her. Now he asks husbands to love their wives with that same care. He says that husband and wife become "one flesh," that is, a very deep union. Then he compares that union with the union of Christ and his church.

For today: care for the people close to you as you care for yourself. This week, ask yourself what your wife, your family, or a brother in the church needs, and attend to it with one concrete act of kindness.
exp.5:15:
It says that, in addition to everything mentioned before, we must take up the shield of faith. With that shield we can quench the fiery darts of the wicked one, that is, of the devil. The fiery darts are attacks that aim to wound or destroy, such as doubts, fear, temptation, or accusations. The phrase "above all" here means "in addition to everything" or "in any case," not that faith is more important than the rest.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus, probably from prison. He uses the image of a Roman soldier to explain that the life of faith is a spiritual struggle. Each piece of the armor represents something God gives: truth, righteousness, peace, faith, salvation, and his Word. Interpreters differ on the details of each symbol, but the central message is clear: we must stand firm, trusting in God.

When a thought of fear or guilt comes, do not face it alone in your own strength. Respond with confidence in what God has promised, and pray, asking him for help.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that God saves us by his grace, that is, by his undeserved favor, and that we receive it through faith, which means trusting in Jesus. The word "are" in the King James wording means "you are," and "boast" means "brag about oneself." What follows, "and that not of yourselves," is commonly understood to mean that the whole of salvation, including the faith, is a gift from God; some scholars think "it" refers only to the salvation. In either case, the point is that we did not earn it.

The apostle Paul writes to believers in Ephesus, who were mostly not of Jewish background. He reminds them that they were once spiritually dead, and that God, out of love, raised them up together with Christ. He wants them to understand that their new life is God's work and not an achievement of their own.

Today, instead of straining to deserve God's love, rest in the fact that he has already given it to you in Christ. Give thanks, and let that gratitude move you to serve others.
exp.5:23:
Paul wishes that the favor and kindness of God, that is, his grace, be with all who love Jesus Christ in sincerity. The word "sincerity" can also be understood as a love that does not become corrupt or come to an end. The closing note, which says the letter was written from Rome, was added later by copyists; Paul probably did not write it.

Paul concludes his letter to the Christians in Ephesus. Earlier he explained that Tychicus, his co-worker, would bring them news from him to encourage them. Paul writes as a prisoner, and yet he closes with a blessing for all believers, not just for some.

Today, grace is not earned through outward appearances; it accompanies the one who truly loves Jesus. This week, examine your love for him calmly: is it steady and sincere, or merely a habit? Bring it to him in prayer, trusting in his grace.
exp.0:5:
This verse says that everything God did for us has a purpose: that his grace be praised and his glory be seen. "Accepted" is an older word meaning received, taken in with favor. "The Beloved" is Jesus Christ, the Son whom the Father loves. God welcomed us with affection through Jesus, not because of our merits.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus, probably while he was in prison. He has been speaking about how God chose them and adopted them as children. Here he sums up that plan with a song of praise: everything springs from grace, that is, from a favor that cannot be earned. Then, in the next verse, he speaks of redemption through the blood of Christ.

For today: when you feel you do not measure up, remember that your worth before God does not depend on your performance, but on Christ. Rest in that acceptance and respond with gratitude, giving God the credit for whatever is good in your life.
exp.5:0:
They say children should obey their parents, and that they do so "in the Lord," meaning as part of their faith in Christ. The phrase "in the Lord" is rendered here as it appears in the verse. Some scholars note that the words "in the Lord" could be understood in two ways: obeying as an act of faithfulness to Christ, or obeying in what agrees with the will of the Lord. The word "right" means correct, something that is good before God.

The apostle Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Ephesus. In this part he explains how to live the new life in Christ within the family. Before this verse he speaks of husbands and wives, and here he addresses children directly, treating them as an important part of the community of faith.

For today: obeying your parents with respect, even when it is hard, is a concrete way to honor God. If you are a father or mother, remember that this authority is exercised with love and care.
exp.3:6:
It says that God gives grace to each believer, leaving no one out. It is given according to the measure of Christ's gift, that is, according to what Christ decides to distribute. Each one receives what is theirs.

Paul writes this letter to believers, and in the verses before, he stresses unity: one Lord, one faith, one God. Here he shifts a little: although we are one, we are not all the same. Each person receives a different grace for serving. Then Paul quotes a psalm about Christ, who ascends to heaven and distributes gifts. Scholars explain that quotation in several ways, but the central idea is clear.

Today you might ask yourself, "What has God given me to help others?" Do not compare yourself with anyone. Use joyfully what you have received, in your family or in your church.
exp.3:22:
This verse says that believers must be renewed in the spirit of their mind. The word "renewed" means becoming new, being changed from the inside. The phrase "the spirit of your mind" speaks of the deep way we think, feel, and decide.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus, most of whom were not Jewish by background. He reminds them that, having come to know Christ, they learned to put off the old way of living and to put on the new self. This verse joins both ideas: the change in conduct begins with a renewed mind. Some understand this renewal to be the work of the Holy Spirit, while others understand that it also involves our own effort; the text does not spell this out.

Today, before you react with anger or with lies, stop and pray. Ask God to help you think the way Jesus thinks, and feed your mind on his Word every day.
exp.3:9:
This verse says that Jesus, the one who came down to earth, is the same one who afterward went up "far above all the heavens." He did this so that he might "fill all things," that is, to fill everything with his presence and his work.

Paul writes to the church in Ephesus. He speaks of the unity of the body of Christ and quotes Psalm 68 to show that Christ triumphed and gave gifts. Some understand the lower parts of the earth as his incarnation and death; others understand it as his descent into the tomb. Then Paul explains that these gifts are people who serve the church.

Today, remember that Christ, who humbled himself to the lowest place, now reigns over all. If he has given you gifts, use them with humility to serve and build up others.
exp.2:13:
Paul says that he kneels before God the Father, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Bowing the knees is a way of saying that he prays with humility and reverence. The words "for this cause" direct us to look at what he has just explained.

Paul writes from prison to the believers in Ephesus. He has just said that Jews and non-Jews now form one people in Christ and can approach God with confidence. For that reason he begins to pray for them. Some think that "for this cause" picks up what he said at the start of chapter 3, before explaining his ministry; the text allows for this.

Today, when you feel small or tired, remember that you have free access to the Father through Christ. Pray for others with humility and without hurry, as Paul did, whatever your posture is, whether standing, sitting, or kneeling.
exp.3:20:
Paul says to the believers in Ephesus: "if indeed you heard Christ and were taught by him, as the truth is in Jesus." Paul does not doubt them; some read the "if" as "since." The truth is not only an idea, but is seen in the person and life of Jesus.

Paul writes this letter to Christians of non-Jewish origin. He has just described the pagans, who live without conscience and give themselves over to impurity. With this verse he reminds them that they learned something very different when they came to know Christ, and this prepares the call to leave the former way of life.

For today: it is not enough to know facts from the Bible. Ask yourself whether what you learn from Jesus is shaping the way you speak, work, and treat others. Choose one concrete habit to change today, in the light of how Jesus lived.
exp.4:3:
This verse says that believers should not use filthy words, meaning coarse or obscene language. Nor should they use foolish talk, which is silly or worthless conversation, or crude jesting, which were rough jokes or jokes with a double meaning. It says these things "are not convenient." Instead, we should speak with thanksgiving, that is, with gratitude to God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Ephesus. He has just asked them to walk in love, as Christ loved us. That is why he speaks of living as "saints," set apart for God, and of caring for both their conduct and their words. Scholars debate how far the word "jesting" reaches, but the general meaning is clear.

For today: before you joke or comment on something, ask yourself whether that joke builds someone up or puts them down. Try each day to say out loud something you are thankful to God for.
exp.3:16:
Paul says he gives this command with the authority of the Lord: believers must no longer live as the Gentiles do, that is, as those who do not know God.

Paul writes to the church in Ephesus, made up of Jews and Gentiles. He has just spoken about growing together in Christ and in love. Now he contrasts this new life with the old one. The verses that follow explain that a mind without God is darkened and the heart becomes hardened.

For today: before deciding something, ask yourself whether you are thinking with the mind of Christ or with the ideas that are fashionable. Spend a few minutes in the Bible and in prayer so that God renews your way of thinking.
exp.1:21:
It says that you, the believers, are being built together, like stones of one house, so that God may dwell in it through his Spirit.

Paul writes to Christians in Ephesus, many of whom were not Jewish. He reminds them that they are no longer strangers, but part of God's family. He uses the image of a temple: Christ is the chief cornerstone, and the apostles and prophets are the foundation. Paul wants them to understand that Jews and non-Jews form one people.

For today: do not live your faith in isolation. Look for a church or community where you can serve, learn, and support others. God works in a special way when his children are united, and you are a valuable stone in that house.

sum.4: Paul calls believers to imitate God and to live in love, just as Christ gave himself up for us. He encourages them to leave behind the works of darkness, to walk as children of light, to make the most of their time, and to be filled with the Spirit. He then teaches mutual submission, and that husbands should love their wives as Christ loved the church.
sum.2: Paul, a prisoner for Christ, explains that God revealed a mystery to him: that the Gentiles are also heirs and members of the same body through the gospel. This wisdom of God is shown through the church. He then prays that they would be strengthened by the Spirit, that Christ would dwell in their hearts, and that they would know his immense love.
sum.1: Paul reminds us that we were dead in sin, but God, out of his great love, made us alive with Christ. We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and we were created to do good. Christ broke down the wall between Jews and non-Jews, and now all of us form one family, a temple where God dwells.
sum.3: Paul, a prisoner for the Lord, urges believers to live with humility, patience, and love, taking care to keep the unity that the Spirit gives. Christ gave different gifts to his Church so that it would grow mature and united in love. He teaches them to put off the old way of life and put on the new: to speak the truth, not to hold on to anger, to work honestly, and to be kind and forgiving, just as God forgave them.
sum.0: Paul greets the believers in Ephesus and praises God because, in Christ, God chose them, adopted them as his children, forgave them through his blood, and sealed them with the Holy Spirit. He then prays that they will understand the hope God has given and the great power of God, who raised Christ from the dead and placed him as head over the church, which is his body.
sum.5: Paul teaches how to live in the family and at work: children honor their parents, fathers raise their children without provoking them to anger, and servants and masters act as though serving the Lord. He then calls believers to put on the armor of God to stand against evil, praying at all times. He closes by sending Tychicus with greetings of peace and grace.
